title: Minimax on a game tree
objectives: Code minimax and find the value of a small game.

screens.title: Twenty-one sticks
screens.prose: Two players take turns removing 1, 2 or 3 sticks from a pile. Whoever takes the last stick wins. A position is the number of sticks left when it is your turn. With 0 left, the player before you took the last one.
screens.question: Tap every pile size from 0 to 12 where the player to move loses against best play.

hints.text: With 0 sticks you have already lost. With 1, 2 or 3 you take them all.
With 4, every move leaves 1, 2 or 3 for your opponent.
A losing pile is one where every move hands the opponent a winning pile.

feedback.correct: Piles 0, 4, 8 and 12 lose: every move leaves the opponent a pile that wins.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work up from 0: a pile wins if some move reaches a losing pile.

byKey.odd: You marked 1, 5 and 9. From those, taking 1 leaves 0, 4 or 8, which lose for the opponent.

explain.text: From a multiple of 4, any take of 1 to 3 leaves a pile that is not a multiple of 4. From any other pile, you can take the remainder and hand back a multiple of 4.

screens.title: The first move from 21
screens.prose: The pattern goes on: the losing piles are the multiples of 4. The game starts with 21 sticks and you move first.
screens.question: How many sticks should you take?

hints.text: Which multiple of 4 is just below 21?

feedback.correct: Take 1 and leave 20, a multiple of 4; then always take 4 minus what they took.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Leave your opponent a multiple of 4.

byKey.three: That leaves 18, which is not a multiple of 4: they take 2 and leave you 16.
byKey.two: That leaves 19: they take 3 and leave you 16.

explain.text: Take 1: leaving 20 means every reply leaves 17, 18 or 19, and you restore a multiple of 4. The first player wins with best play.

screens.title: Backing up a tree
screens.prose: Name the steps we used. At a **max** node you pick the largest child value; at a **min** node your opponent picks the smallest. Leaves are **terminal values**, here your payoff. Values passed up are **backed-up values**: this is **minimax**.
screens.question: You move first (branch a, b or c), then your opponent picks 1, 2 or 3. What is the value at the root?

hints.text: Back up each min node first.
Branch a gives min(3, 9, 6) = 3; do b and c.
The root takes the largest of 3, 1 and 4.

feedback.correct: Min nodes give 3, 1 and 4; you take c, worth 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Your opponent picks the smallest leaf under each branch.

byKey.helps: You took the best leaf anywhere, as if your opponent helped you. Under c they choose 4.
byKey.worst: That is the smallest leaf overall. You choose the branch, so take the best of the minima.

explain.text: Each min node takes its smallest leaf: 3, 1 and 4. The root takes the largest of those, so branch c is worth 4.

screens.title: The value of tic-tac-toe
screens.prose: Run minimax from the empty tic-tac-toe board, with X maximising (1 win, 0 draw, −1 loss) and O minimising. Our memoised minimax gives the same value after each of X's nine first moves.
screens.question: What is the value of the game?

options.text: 0: a draw with best play, whatever X plays first
1: X wins by taking the centre first
options.why: O can always hold the centre opening to a draw; the value after X's centre move is 0.

options.text: 1 for a corner opening, 0 for the others
options.why: Every first move has value 0 under best replies.
Moving first never hurts in tic-tac-toe; the value is 0.

hints.text: Check the values after each first move.
All nine are 0.
So the root is 0.

feedback.correct: Tic-tac-toe is a draw with best play, and every first move keeps the draw.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Best play from both sides.

explain.text: All nine first moves have minimax value 0, so the game value is 0. Mistakes decide real games, not the opening.

screens.title: How big is the tree?
screens.prose: The full game tree from the empty board has 549,946 nodes, root included, and 255,168 complete games. Yet only 5,478 different boards can arise in play (of the $3^9 = 19{,}683$ ways to fill nine cells). We checked 5,478 by search and by counting legal boards.
screens.question: About how many times does the full tree visit each position? Give the nearest whole number.

hints.text: Divide nodes by positions.
That is about 100.4.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the nodes by the positions.

byKey.games: You divided the games by the positions. Count every node of the tree.
byKey.cells: You divided by $3^9$. Only 5,478 boards are legal.

explain.text: Each position is reached about 100 times by different move orders, so remembering values (a table, as `lru_cache` keeps) turns 549,946 visits into 5,478 evaluations.

screens.title: Code minimax
screens.prose: Write `nim_losing(n)`, then `minimax(board, player)` with `lru_cache` as the table of seen positions, and `count_positions()`. Boards are strings like `'XX.OO....'`, read row by row.
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

tests.call: [n for n in range(20) if nim_losing(n)]

widget.how: Submit runs 9 hidden tests: the losing Nim positions below 20, planted boards with known values, every first move of tic-tac-toe, the 5,478 positions, and a last move that fills the board and wins.

mutants.symptom: A position counts as losing when any move leads to a win for the opponent.
The min node is scored as a max: the opponent helps you.
Counts every visit, not distinct boards: no table of seen positions.
A last move that fills the board and wins is scored as a draw: the full board is checked before the win.

hints.text: A Nim pile loses when every move leaves a winning pile.
Return 1, −1 or 0 at the end of a game; otherwise max for X and min for O.
Count boards with a set, stopping at wins and full boards.

feedback.generic: Some tests fail. Read the first failing row.

screens.title: The opponent is not on your side
screens.prose: O to move on this board. A colleague backs up the min level with a max, "since we want X to win", and reports that X wins.
screens.question: What is the board's true value?

options.text: 1: X wins on the top row
options.why: Only if O lets it. O is to move here and wins at once.
O has a win in one move; best play takes it.

options.text: It depends on who is lucky
options.why: With best play there is no luck: the value is fixed.

hints.text: Whose turn is it?
O plays the right cell of the middle row.
That ends the game: O wins.

feedback.correct: O wins at once: the value is −1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Let O play its best move.

byKey.xwins: You scored O's move as if O wanted X to win. A min node takes the smallest value.

explain.text: A min node takes the worst outcome for you, because your opponent chooses it. Treating it as a max credits you with a win the opponent will never allow.

screens.title: Prefer the quicker win
screens.prose: Two moves both win for X: one wins now (depth 1), the other at depth 3. Plain minimax scores both 1, so it may dawdle. Scoring a win as $10 - \text{depth}$ (depth in moves from now) prefers the short one.
screens.question: What does a win found at depth 3 score?

hints.text: Use $10 - \text{depth}$.
Depth 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the depth from 10.

byKey.add: You added the depth. Later wins must score less.

explain.text: An immediate win (depth 1) scores 9 and this one 7, so the search takes the win now. A loss is scored $-(10 - \text{depth})$, so a forced loss is put off as long as possible.

screens.title: Minimax
screens.prose: For a two-player, zero-sum game of perfect information: $$V(s) = \begin{cases} \text{payoff} & s \text{ terminal} \\ \max_a V(s') & \text{you to move} \\ \min_a V(s') & \text{opponent to move} \end{cases}$$ It is `graphs-dp` l17's backward induction with an opponent who minimises. Games with hidden information or mixed strategies come in `game-theory` l5.
screens.question: What does memoising minimax change?

options.text: The work: each position is valued once
The value: it finds better moves
options.why: The value is the same; it is only computed once per position.
The tree is the same; repeats are looked up.

feedback.correct: Same values, far less work: 5,478 positions instead of 549,946 nodes.

screens.title: Alternating offers
screens.prose: Two desks negotiate a block trade in alternating moves. You open with offer a or b; they respond with 1 or 2. Your profit in £k at each end is shown.
screens.question: With both sides playing best, what profit do you lock in, in £k?

hints.text: They pick the end worse for you.
a gives 3, b gives 5.
Choose b.

feedback.correct: Offer b: they hold you to 5, better than the 3 after a.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Back up their choice first.

byKey.greedy: You aimed at the 8 under a. They answer with 2 and leave you 3.
byKey.avg: You averaged. A rival does not choose at random.

explain.text: Backing up their replies gives 3 after a and 5 after b, so you offer b and lock in £5k. Bargaining games with hidden values need the tools of `game-theory`.

ideas: Minimax backs values up a game tree: max at your moves, min at your opponent's, payoffs at the leaves.
In 21-stick Nim the losing piles are the multiples of 4, so the first player takes 1; tic-tac-toe is a draw (value 0) after every first move.
The full tic-tac-toe tree has 549,946 nodes and 255,168 games but only 5,478 positions; a table of seen positions values each once.

formula.name: Minimax
formula.note: Payoffs at terminal positions; two players, zero-sum, perfect information.

summary.trap: Scoring a min node as if the opponent helps you: it takes the worst outcome for you.

quiz.prose: Nim with 17 sticks, take 1 to 3, last stick wins. You move.
quiz.question: How many sticks should you take?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Leave a multiple of 4.

explain.text: From 17, taking 1 leaves 16, a losing pile for your opponent.

quiz.prose: A max root has two min children. The first has leaves 2 and 8; the second has leaves 5 and 4.
quiz.question: What is the root's value?

feedback.correct: Min nodes give 2 and 4; the root takes 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Back up the min nodes first.

byKey.max: Your opponent will not let you reach 8.
byKey.min: You choose the branch: take the better minimum.

explain.text: The min nodes are 2 and 4, and the root takes the larger, 4.

quiz.question: Why does a table of seen positions help so much in tic-tac-toe?

options.text: The same board recurs by many move orders
It prunes the moves that cannot matter
options.why: That is alpha-beta, the next lesson.

options.text: It replaces search with a rule of thumb
It plays the first legal move
options.why: It stores values; it does not choose blindly.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count nodes against positions.

explain.text: The full tree has about 100 nodes for every legal board, so storing each board's value removes almost all the work.
